newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Amnesty hits UN refugee agency over Hutu expulsions.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty hits UN refugee agency over Hutu expulsions.

text.p: Amnesty International accused the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR on Friday of betraying its founding principles by encouraging the expulsion of hundreds of thousands of refugees in central Africa.

And in a new report, it warned that mass returns of Hutu refugees to Rwanda and Burundi would not end the crisis and could be followed by fresh explosions of ethnic hatred that would lead to another exodus.
The London-based human rights group said the UNHCR "legitimised" deportations by ignoring questions over the safety of returnees and whether they went back of their own free will.
Half a million Rwandan Hutus in Tanzania were expelled by troops in December just weeks after they got their marching orders from the government and the UNHCR in a joint communique.

They followed the return home of 600,000 Rwandan Hutus and 60,000 Burundian Hutus from eastern Zaire after their camps were overrun by rebels, ending the refugee crisis that has haunted the central African region for nearly three years.
Amnesty said Rwanda was not safe. Last year was marked by a sharp rise in killings by the Tutsi army and its opponents with 650 civilians dead from April-July and at least 250 in August.
"These critical questions were overlooked or given short shrift in the rush to meet the arbitrary deadline," it said.

Analysts in the region have long argued the mass returns were wanted by host countries tired of the economic and social problems the refugees created and by an international community paying $1 million a day to maintain the sprawling camps.

Even the Rwandan government, dominated by the Tutsi minority which took power after the 1994 Hutu-led genocide, left no doubt it believed force had to be used to break the stranglehold hardline leaders held on the refugees and bring them home.
Amnesty said forced repatriation violated UNHCR's core mandate -- to defend the right to asylum and ensure that the return home of refugees was voluntary.
Asked for comment on the report, Augustine Mahiga, a senior UNHCR official who is in charge of the Great Lakes region, said his agency had few options over the course it took.
"We were increasingly marginalised by donors who got very impatient with refugees. They even saw us as an obstacle to returns because of our traditional mandate," he told Reuters.
In Rwanda UNHCR's dilemma was how to interpret its obligation to protect refugees, many of whom did not flee persecution so much as possible prosecution for the genocide.
Amnesty said Rwandan jails were stuffed with 92,000 Hutu genocide suspects and that its government had not demonstrated a clear commitment to human rights protection.

"The rushed and forced nature of returns may well lead to increased violations," it said. "In those circumstances, and given the legacy of Rwanda's horrifying record of human rights abuse, decisions about refugee protection and return must be taken with the greatest of care and caution."

Amnesty said ethnic conflict and rights violations would trigger new refugee crises in a region where the seeds of hatred between the majority Hutu and minority Tutsi tribes go back centuries, repeatedly erupting into waves of violence.

"Although international focus and concern have faded, central Africa's refugee tragedy is far from over. The situation in both Burundi and eastern Zaire continues to be explosive. In fact, if conditions worsen, a mass exodus of refugees -- most likely into Tanzania -- is expected," it added.
